paper.title: Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2
paper.abstract: All of life encodes information with DNA. Although tools for genome sequencing, synthesis and editing have transformed biological research, we still lack sufficient understanding of the immense complexity encoded by genomes to predict the effects of many classes of genomic changes or to intelligently compose new biological systems. Artificial intelligence models that learn information from genomic sequences across diverse organisms have increasingly advanced prediction and design capabilities1,2. Here we introduce Evo 2, a biological foundation model trained on 9 trillion DNA base pairs from a highly curated genomic atlas spanning all domains of life to have a 1 million token context window with single-nucleotide resolution. Evo 2 learns to accurately predict the functional impacts of genetic variation—from noncoding pathogenic mutations to clinically significant BRCA1 variants—without task-specific fine-tuning. Mechanistic interpretability analyses reveal that Evo 2 learns representations associated with biological features, including exon–intron boundaries, transcription factor binding sites, protein structural elements and prophage genomic regions. The generative abilities of Evo 2 produce mitochondrial, prokaryotic and eukaryotic sequences at genome scale with greater naturalness and coherence than previous methods. Evo 2 also generates experimentally validated chromatin accessibility patterns when guided by predictive models3,4 and inference-time search. We have made Evo 2 fully open, including model parameters, training code5, inference code and the OpenGenome2 dataset, to accelerate the exploration and design of biological complexity. Evo 2 is an artificial intelligence-based biological foundation model trained on 9 trillion DNA base pairs spanning all domains of life that predicts functional properties from genomic sequences and provides a rich generative model for researchers in biology.
paper.tldr: Built a DNA foundation model across all domains of life that predicts the functional impact of mutations without fine-tuning, reveals interpretable biological features, and generates coherent genome-scale sequences including experimentally validated chromatin accessibility patterns.
paper.why: Evo 2 is a genome-scale foundation model trained on 9 trillion bases spanning all domains of life, with a 1Mbp context, zero-shot prediction of variant effects (including BRCA1), mechanistic interpretability, genome-scale generation with experimental validation, and full openness of model, code, and data. It defines a new capability class for DNA modeling and design that the whole field can immediately reuse. It edges out its predecessor Evo and other strong candidates on scale, generality, and openness.

summary.tldr: Evo 2 is an open 7B/40B-parameter DNA foundation model (StripedHyena 2 architecture) trained on 9.3 trillion tokens across all domains of life with 1-Mb context and single-nucleotide resolution, enabling zero-shot variant-effect prediction, interpretable genomic features, and genome-scale generation including experimentally validated chromatin accessibility design.
summary.background: Genomic language models have so far been mostly prokaryote-only or short-context, handling eukaryotic gene regulation, long-range interactions, and indels poorly. A generalist model is hard to build because it requires curated data spanning all of life, architectures efficient at million-base contexts, and evaluation without task-specific labels.
summary.approach: The authors trained Evo 2 7B (2.4T tokens) and 40B (9.3T tokens) on OpenGenome2 (~8.8T nucleotides from bacteria, archaea, eukarya, phage; eukaryotic-infecting virus sequences excluded), using two-phase training (8,192-token pretraining, then midtraining to 1M context) with the StripedHyena 2 multi-hybrid convolution architecture (~3x throughput vs Transformers at 1M context, 40B scale). They evaluated zero-shot likelihoods for mutation effects, trained a Batch-TopK sparse autoencoder on layer-26 representations (1B tokens) for interpretability, generated genomes autoregressively, and used beam search guided by an Enformer/Borzoi ensemble to design DNA with specified chromatin accessibility.
findings: Zero-shot on ClinVar, Evo 2 was best of all methods tested on coding and noncoding non-SNVs (indels/duplications), which AlphaMissense and GPN-MSA cannot score, though it trailed ESM-1b/GPN-MSA on coding SNVs.
A ridge classifier on Evo 2 40B embeddings classified BRCA1 loss-of-function variants at AUROC 0.95 / AUPRC 0.88 (n=789 test set); zero-shot it beat all models on BRCA1 noncoding SNVs.

SAE features align with prophages, exon-intron boundaries, TF binding motifs (recalling 70% of HOCOMOCO promoter motifs vs 35% for HOMER), and protein secondary structure, and transfer to woolly mammoth sequence.

Generation: 580-kb M. genitalium genomes where ~70% of predicted genes have Pfam hits (vs 18% for Evo 1), plus human mitochondrial genomes with correct CDS/tRNA/rRNA counts and ~330-kb yeast chromosome sequences with intronic genes.

Designed 1-4 kb chromatin accessibility patterns validated by ATAC-seq in human cells: 33/36 designs (92%) reached AUROC > 0.8 within-sequence, while cell-type-specific designs were harder (4/24 with >2-fold differential accessibility).
summary.why: For transcriptomics and multiomics, Evo 2 provides single-nucleotide-resolution embeddings spanning promoter-to-distal regulatory distances, useful for interpreting regulatory variants, annotating non-model species, and as inputs to lightweight supervised heads for splicing, expression, or chromatin phenotypes. Its coupling of a general sequence generator with sequence-to-function oracles (Enformer/Borzoi) via inference-time search is a reusable template for designing regulatory DNA with controllable epigenomic outcomes.
summary.limitations: Generated genomes are not shown to be functional (essential genes are missing, nothing replication-tested), and prediction still trails supervised models on distal regulatory variants (DART-eval caQTL AUROC 0.58 vs 0.77 for ChromBPNet) and on protein deep mutational scanning. Human gene essentiality prediction is modest (AUROC 0.66), and the model was trained without any human variation or functional genomics data.

also.title: A foundation model of transcription across human cell types
also.abstract: Transcriptional regulation, involving the complex interplay between regulatory sequences and proteins, directs all biological processes. Computational models of transcription lack generalizability to accurately extrapolate in unseen cell types and conditions. Here, we introduce GET, an interpretable foundation model designed to uncover regulatory grammars across 213 human fetal and adult cell types. Relying exclusively on chromatin accessibility data and sequence information, GET achieves experimental-level accuracy in predicting gene expression even in previously unseen cell types. GET showcases remarkable adaptability across new sequencing platforms and assays, enabling regulatory inference across a broad range of cell types and conditions, and uncovering universal and cell type specific transcription factor interaction networks. We evaluated its performance on prediction of regulatory activity, inference of regulatory elements and regulators, and identification of physical interactions between transcription factors. Specifically, we show GET outperforms current models in predicting lentivirus-based massive parallel reporter assay readout with reduced input data. In fetal erythroblasts, we identify distal (>1Mbp) regulatory regions that were missed by previous models. In B cells, we identified a lymphocyte-specific transcription factor-transcription factor interaction that explains the functional significance of a leukemia-risk predisposing germline mutation. In sum, we provide a generalizable and accurate model for transcription together with catalogs of gene regulation and transcription factor interactions, all with cell type specificity.

summary.tldr: GET is an interpretable transformer foundation model trained on scATAC-seq chromatin accessibility from 213 human fetal and adult cell types that predicts gene expression at experimental-level accuracy in unseen cell types and yields cell-type-specific regulatory element and TF interaction catalogs.
summary.background: Computational models of transcription (Expecto, Basenji2, Enformer) must be fine-tuned on the cell type of interest, so they generalize poorly to unseen cell types and conditions. The core difficulty is learning how regulatory sequences and TFs drive transcription from largely unpaired, cell-type-specific chromatin and expression data.
summary.approach: GET uses a two-stage design: self-supervised masked pretraining on pseudobulk scATAC-seq (peak-by-TF-motif matrices, 200 peaks ≈ 2–4 Mbp regions, 282 motif clusters) across 213 cell types (1.3M single nuclei), then fine-tuning on the 153 cell types with paired RNA-seq to predict expression, using an Enformer-like architecture (embedding layer + 12 attention layers; ~8h fine-tuning on 8 A100s; LoRA option). Interpretation of the fine-tuned model yields motif/region contribution scores, causal TF–TF interaction discovery (LiNGAM), and an AlphaFold2-based structural interaction catalog (1,718 TF pairs).
findings: Predicting expression in leave-out fetal astrocytes, GET reached Pearson r = 0.94 (R2 = 0.88), comparable to experimental replicate concordance, versus r = 0.51 for gene activity scores and r = 0.83 for the most similar training cell type.

Zero-shot on K562 lentiMPRA (226,243 sequences), GET predictions correlated r = 0.55 (with accessibility) vs Enformer's r = 0.44 with much worse dynamic range (slope 0.14 vs 0.63), and screened all elements in the compute Enformer needed for 2,000.
On fetal erythroblast HbF loci and K562 CRISPRi benchmarks, GET outperformed Enformer, HyenaDNA, DeepSEA and ABC especially for distal (>100 kb, up to >1 Mbp) enhancer–promoter inference.
Top-ranked causal TF–TF predictions matched STRING physical interactions at 25.2% precision (vs 5.6% random), comparable to mass-spectrometry atlases.

A case study found a lymphocyte-specific PAX5–nuclear receptor (NR2C2) interaction mediated by the PAX5 octapeptide IDR, validated by proximity labeling, and showed the leukemia-risk G183S germline mutation strengthens this interaction with a G183S-specific transcriptional signature in B-ALL patients.
summary.why: For multiomics researchers, GET shows that ATAC accessibility plus sequence alone (no transcriptome in pretraining) can support zero-shot expression prediction and regulatory inference across assays, platforms and unseen cell types, including tumors. The released GET Catalog and its motif-contribution interpretation framework offer transferable machinery for variant-to-regulation mapping and TF co-regulation discovery that complements single-cell transcriptome foundation models like scGPT/Geneformer.
summary.limitations: GET uses region-level (not nucleotide-level) inputs, cannot distinguish TF homologs with near-identical motifs, and is trained only on pseudobulk normal cell states without 3D chromatin, TF expression, or perturbation/disease data in pretraining. Variant impact prediction and kinetic/temporal regulation remain open areas.

also.title: Sequence modeling and design from molecular to genome scale with Evo
also.abstract: The genome is a sequence that completely encodes the DNA, RNA, and proteins that orchestrate the function of a whole organism. Advances in machine learning combined with massive datasets of whole genomes could enable a biological foundation model that accelerates the mechanistic understanding and generative design of complex molecular interactions. We report Evo, a genomic foundation model that enables prediction and generation tasks from the molecular to genome scale. Using an architecture based on advances in deep signal processing, we scale Evo to 7 billion parameters with a context length of 131 kilobases (kb) at single-nucleotide, byte resolution. Trained on whole prokaryotic genomes, Evo can generalize across the three fundamental modalities of the central dogma of molecular biology to perform zero-shot function prediction that is competitive with, or outperforms, leading domain-specific language models. Evo also excels at multi-element generation tasks, which we demonstrate by generating synthetic CRISPR-Cas molecular complexes and entire transposable systems for the first time. Using information learned over whole genomes, Evo can also predict gene essentiality at nucleotide resolution and can generate coding-rich sequences up to 650 kb in length, orders of magnitude longer than previous methods. Advances in multi-modal and multi-scale learning with Evo provides a promising path toward improving our understanding and control of biology across multiple levels of complexity.

also.title: Spatial transcriptomic clocks reveal cell proximity effects in brain ageing
also.abstract: Old age is associated with a decline in cognitive function and an increase in neurodegenerative disease risk1. Brain ageing is complex and is accompanied by many cellular changes2. Furthermore, the influence that aged cells have on neighbouring cells and how this contributes to tissue decline is unknown. More generally, the tools to systematically address this question in ageing tissues have not yet been developed. Here we generate a spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomics brain atlas of 4.2 million cells from 20 distinct ages across the adult lifespan and across two rejuvenating interventions—exercise and partial reprogramming. We build spatial ageing clocks, machine learning models trained on this spatial transcriptomics atlas, to identify spatial and cell-type-specific transcriptomic fingerprints of ageing, rejuvenation and disease, including for rare cell types. Using spatial ageing clocks and deep learning, we find that T cells, which increasingly infiltrate the brain with age, have a marked pro-ageing proximity effect on neighbouring cells. Surprisingly, neural stem cells have a strong pro-rejuvenating proximity effect on neighbouring cells. We also identify potential mediators of the pro-ageing effect of T cells and the pro-rejuvenating effect of neural stem cells on their neighbours. These results suggest that rare cell types can have a potent influence on their neighbours and could be targeted to counter tissue ageing. Spatial ageing clocks represent a useful tool for studying cell–cell interactions in spatial contexts and should allow scalable assessment of the efficacy of interventions for ageing and disease. A spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomics map of the mouse brain at different ages reveals signatures of ageing, rejuvenation and disease, including ageing effects associated with T cells and rejuvenation associated with neural stem cells.

summary.tldr: The authors built a 4.2-million-cell MERFISH spatial transcriptomics atlas of the ageing mouse brain across the lifespan, and using 'spatial ageing clocks' and graph neural networks they show that rare cell types exert strong neighbourhood effects: T cells make nearby cells transcriptomically older (likely via IFNγ), while neural stem cells make them younger (possibly via exosomes), with exercise modifying both effects.
summary.background: Brain ageing involves coordinated changes across many cell types, but how aged or rejuvenated cells influence their neighbours spatially is unknown. Existing spatial transcriptomics studies had either single-cell spatial resolution or temporal coverage, not both, and lacked computational tools to quantify cell-cell spatial interactions during ageing.
summary.approach: They generated a MERFISH atlas (300-gene panel, Vizgen MERSCOPE) of 4.2M cells from male mouse brains: 2.3M cells across 20 lifespan ages (3.4-34.5 months) in coronal sections plus sagittal sections, and added intervention datasets (~900k cells for voluntary exercise; >1M cells for partial OSKM reprogramming). They trained cell-type-specific 'spatial ageing clocks' using a SpatialSmooth procedure (iterative smoothing of expression over a same-type spatial graph) and a GNN to predict neighbourhood ageing from cell-type composition and connectivity. Cross-dataset imputation via TISSUE expanded the 300-gene panel to ~12,000 genes for mediator discovery.
findings: Ageing changed cell proportions: T cells strongly increased (r=0.72) and NSCs strongly decreased (r=-0.93); microglia had the most age-changed genes, and white matter (CC/ACO) was the largest ageing hotspot.
Spatial ageing clocks reached R>0.7 in 14 of 18 cell types (clock sizes 62-292 genes) and generalized to external datasets, female mice, sagittal sections, and scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq.

Interventions: exercise rejuvenated vasculature cells (endothelial -4.9 months, VSMCs -4.7 months, pericytes -3.4 months), while partial reprogramming rejuvenated NSCs (-2.7 months) and neuroblasts (-2.8 months) but aged some glial cells.

Proximity analysis across 214 cell-cell pairs showed T cells have the strongest pro-ageing effect (especially on oligodendrocytes/pericytes) and NSCs the strongest pro-rejuvenating effect, confirmed by in silico GNN gain/loss-of-function perturbations and robust to spatial permutation, gene spillover, and inflammation-state controls.

Mediators: IFNγ signalling mediates the T cell effect (STAT1 immunofluorescence elevated near T cells, e.g. p=0.0078 in cortex), while exosome/fatty-acid-oxidation markers (CD9, CPT1A) are enriched in and near NSCs, respectively.
Application to disease models (LPS inflammation, Alzheimer's TauPS2APP, EAE and localized demyelination) showed accelerated transcriptomic ageing in most cell types, with microglia prominent.
summary.why: Spatial ageing clocks and GNN-based proximity analysis provide a scalable computational framework for measuring tissue ageing, intervention efficacy, and cell-type-specific spatial interactions at single-cell resolution—a template directly relevant to spatial transcriptomics and cell-state models in other tissues. For an AI-omics reader, SpatialSmooth (spatial-graph smoothing for ageing clocks) and in silico cell-type perturbation via GNNs on spatial neighbourhoods are the transferable methodological contributions.
summary.limitations: The 300-gene panel limits resolution and required computational imputation (TISSUE) to identify mediators, which are correlative rather than causally validated. Only male mice, a single tissue (mouse brain), and small intervention cohorts (n=4 per group) constrain generalization.
